summary.en: Use a type-based reference for printf and scanf, including bases, length modifiers and pointers.
summary.bn: টাইপভিত্তিক রেফারেন্স দিয়ে printf ও scanf-এর ভিত্তি, দৈর্ঘ্যের মডিফায়ার ও পয়েন্টার ফরম্যাট ব্যবহার করো।

notes: C99 standardized useful additions including ll, j, z, t and hexadecimal floating conversions. The tables describe C17 behavior. C23 adds further facilities, so an older compiler accepting a format extension should not be treated as proof that it belongs to C17.

examples.title: Signed and unsigned integer families
examples.explanationHtml: %d and %i are equivalent for output; unsigned 26 appears as 1a in hex and 32 in octal.

examples.title: Floating, character and string families
examples.explanationHtml: For printf, %f and %lf both consume double; %e uses an exponent and %g chooses a compact representation.

examples.title: A size value
examples.explanationHtml: %zu matches the unsigned size_t type rather than assuming it is int or long.

examples.title: Input base detection
examples.explanationHtml: %i recognizes 032 as octal 26, while %d reads 032 as decimal 32.

examples.title: Mistake: a wrong size format
examples.explanationHtml: size_t is not int on this host; %zu expresses its type portably and avoids a format mismatch.

examples.title: Object pointer formatting
examples.explanationHtml: %p receives a void * obtained from an object pointer. The address text is implementation-defined and varies between runs; the saved transcript is one real run, not a fixed address guarantee.
examples.outputNote: Object addresses vary between runs and %p spelling is implementation-defined; the .out file records one actual run.

practice.title: Print bases
practice.statementHtml:
Read unsigned n 0 to 255; output Input: then u=U x=X o=O and newline, no prefixes.

Write the exact prompt Input: with one space after the colon, then the stated result with its final newline. The input domain is part of the task; no other output is required for these tests.
hints: Hex and octal output conversions still take unsigned int.

practice.title: Decimal and exponent
practice.statementHtml:

Write the exact prompt Input: with one space after the colon, then the stated result with its final newline. The input domain is part of the task; no other output is required for these tests.
hints: Input needs l; output %e takes double.

practice.statementHtml:

practice.title: Mixed-format record
practice.statementHtml:
Read unsigned roll 0 to 999, double CGPA 0 to 4 and a word 1 to 7 characters; output Input: then R V S on one line with CGPA two decimals.

Write the exact prompt Input: with one space after the colon, then the stated result with its final newline. The input domain is part of the task; no other output is required for these tests.
hints: Match each conversion against its own argument type.

quiz.prompt: How do %d and %i differ for printf?
options: They both print signed decimal int
quiz.explanation: The difference is in scanf base recognition, not printf output.

quiz.prompt: Which scanf conversion recognizes 0x prefixes for an int?
quiz.explanation: %i detects the base from the input prefix.
Convert an object pointer to void * for the %p argument.

quiz.prompt: What type does scanf %p require as its destination argument?
quiz.explanation: The conversion stores a void * value through its destination address.

quiz.prompt: What is printf %lf equivalent to in C17?
quiz.explanation: For floating printf conversions, l has no effect; L selects long double.

quiz.prompt: Which conversion is appropriate for size_t?
quiz.explanation: The z length modifier expresses size_t without a platform-specific guess.

quiz.prompt: Why can %s input need a width but %s output does not always need one?
options: Input strings never need a terminator
Input must protect destination capacity; output reads an existing terminated string
Input width includes the final null
quiz.explanation: A width limits stored non-null characters; the caller must provide the extra null slot.

examQuestions.question: Compare %d and %i for printf and scanf.
examQuestions.answerHtml: For printf, both print a signed int in decimal. For scanf, %d reads decimal into int *, while %i detects octal and hexadecimal prefixes. Thus input 032 becomes thirty-two with %d and twenty-six with %i.

examQuestions.question: Explain why an I/O reference must distinguish values from destination pointers, using float, size_t and pointer conversions.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
printf consumes values after default promotions, while scanf stores into objects through destination pointers. A float promotes to double for printf %f, but scanf %f requires float * and %lf requires double *. %zu matches size_t output and size_t * input. For output %p pass void *, normally obtained by converting an object pointer; for input %p pass void **. Pointer representations vary, so fixed numeric address output is not a portable test.

Marking: contracts 1, floating distinction 1, size_t 1, pointer types 1, varying output 1.

examQuestions.question: Write a complete C program for this lab task: Read unsigned roll 0 to 999, double CGPA 0 to 4 and a word 1 to 7 characters; output Input: then R V S on one line with CGPA two decimals.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    unsigned int roll;
    double cgpa;
    char room[8];
    printf("Input: ");
    if (scanf("%u %lf %7s", &roll, &cgpa, room) != 3) {
        return 1;
    }
    printf("%03u %.2f %s\n", roll, cgpa, room);
    return 0;
}

Marking: 1 for typed declarations, 1 for checked input, 2 for the required calculation or transformation, and 1 for exact output.
